bull_bear.body:
- Long-term fuel security - GWEL has fuel supply arrangements with South Eastern Coalfields Limited (SECL) and Western Coalfields Limited (WCL), and GKEL with Mahanadi Coalfields Limited (MCL) under Firm Linkage, SHAKTI-II and SHAKTI B-III, each for entire PPA capacity, ensuring reliable coal availability
- Contracted revenue visibility from long-term PPAs, with GWEL achieving 93.9% and GKEL 93.4% of planned power sales under tied-up PPAs
- Best-in-class plant operations - GWEL achieved its highest-ever Plant Load Factor of 84.9% after customer curtailment with machine availability of approximately 94%, and GKEL a PLF of 86.6% with machine availability of approximately 91%
- Brownfield expansion advantage at Kamalanga, where the planned 350 MW Unit 4 benefits from foundations for major equipment and common facilities already developed during earlier phases
- Demonstrated execution capability in smart metering, with approximately 3.9 million smart meters installed and integrated across Uttar Pradesh by April 2026, establishing a foundation for long-term, technology-led and recurring revenue streams
- Recognised operational and safety excellence - GKEL won the CII National Award for Excellence in Energy Management and became the first plant in India to achieve a Platinum Rating under the CII Blue Rating System for Water Management; GWEL was recognised as an Energy Efficient Unit by CII and received the IMC Ramkrishna Bajaj National Quality (RBNQA) Business Excellence Award 2025 with a score of 850
- Strengthened financial flexibility following a Rs 1,200 crore preferential issuance of equity shares and warrants, refinancing of GKEL's senior debt at improved terms, and resolution of GREL's debt through a One-Time Settlement
- Environmental circularity - 100% fly ash utilisation maintained across thermal power plants, and 100% statutory compliance with a 100% ash utilisation rate at both plants
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Dependence on conventional coal-fired thermal generation for the bulk of earnings — The stable earnings base rests on two coal-fired plants (GMR Warora and GMR Kamalanga); the Chairman's message notes India's energy mix is shifting towards renewables, storage and dispatchable solutions even while conventional generation remains critical for grid stability and baseload.
- Offtaker / customer curtailment and DISCOM counterparty exposure — Reported plant load factors at both thermal plants are stated as 'after customer curtailment', and recovery of long-outstanding dues from Haryana DISCOM required favourable Supreme Court judgments — showing that realisation depends on state distribution utilities.
- Legacy litigation, arbitration and contingent liabilities — The Board's Report describes multiple long-running disputes — GKEL vs SEPCO arbitration, GPEL vs NHAI periodic-maintenance arbitration settled through a Conciliation Committee of Independent Experts, and a legacy arbitration contingent liability eliminated only by a Supreme Court judgment — indicating recurring exposure to protracted litigation.
- High leverage and refinancing dependence — Management frames the year around strengthening the balance sheet, resolving legacy obligations through a One-Time Settlement at GREL and refinancing GKEL's senior debt; a further reduction in GKEL's cost of borrowing is stated to be subject to a credit rating upgrade, so financing costs remain rating-dependent.
- Regulatory and judicial stoppage of hydro projects — GMR (Badrinath) Hydro Power's 300 MW Alaknanda project was construction-ready but implementation and financial closure remain stalled by a Supreme Court stay order on 24 hydroelectric projects in Uttarakhand, causing an 11-year delay described as beyond GMR's control.
- Fuel availability and coal price exposure — Both thermal plants depend on long-term fuel supply arrangements (SECL/WCL for GWEL; MCL under Firm Linkage, SHAKTI-II and SHAKTI B-III for GKEL); the Board's Report attributes movement in fuel consumption cost to coal prices during the year.
- Execution and scope risk in the smart metering build-out — The Uttar Pradesh smart metering programme is a large multi-year installation contract with a stated contracted scope against which delivery is still in progress, plus a variation order and further scope-expansion discussions — making revenue recognition contingent on meeting performance obligations.
- Early-stage renewable portfolio with unsecured capacity and offtake — The renewable, hybrid and FDRE initiatives are described by the Chairman as at an early stage; at the planned 350 MW Kamalanga Unit 4 long-term PPAs are secured for only part of the capacity, with efforts continuing to tie up the balance.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body: GPUIL generates and sells electricity from coal-fired thermal power plants at Warora (Maharashtra) and Kamalanga (Odisha), supplying state distribution utilities under long-term power purchase agreements and selling balance power to other customers on a merchant basis, alongside a coal trading business and a solar plant at Charanka, Gujarat. The Company is building a Smart Energy and Digital Utilities business, installing and maintaining smart electricity meters for the State of Uttar Pradesh under the Government's distribution reform programme, and is developing a renewable energy portfolio spanning solar, Commercial & Industrial, hybrid and Firm & Dispatchable Renewable Energy solutions plus hydropower projects in India and Nepal. It also operates three highway assets spanning approximately 888 lane kilometres, undertakes EPC work, and develops urban infrastructure at the GMR Krishnagiri Special Investment Region.

outlook.body:
- Portfolio optimisation through monetisation of select non-core energy assets - advancing the stake sale in the Bajoli Holi Hydro Electricity Plant and the Vemagiri & Rajahmundry gas assets under a framework agreement with Synergy Investments Holding Limited, and using proceeds to address legacy obligations and reduce consolidated debt
- Strengthen the balance sheet and financial flexibility - a preferential issuance of equity shares and warrants aggregating to Rs 1,200 crore, refinancing of GKEL's senior debt at improved terms, and resolution of GREL's debt through a One-Time Settlement
- Simplify the group structure - GMR Energy Limited acquired the residual stake in GKEL, making it a wholly owned subsidiary
- Build a renewable energy portfolio spanning solar, Commercial & Industrial (C&I), hybrid and Firm & Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) solutions, with new entities incorporated to pursue opportunities across multiple states
- Scale the Smart Energy and Digital Utilities business on the back of the Uttar Pradesh smart metering programme, positioned as a foundation for long-term, technology-led and recurring revenue streams
- Grow thermal capacity at an existing brownfield site by adding a 350 MW Unit 4 at the Kamalanga plant, leveraging foundations for major equipment and common facilities already developed in earlier phases
- Pursue the hydro portfolio in a calibrated manner with emphasis on project viability, risk management, capital discipline and long-term value creation - advancing the 900 MW Upper Karnali project in Nepal with strategic partners and requisite approvals
- Monetise urban infrastructure land at GMR Krishnagiri Special Investment Region through land sales and industrial leasing, with 27 acres under discussion for sale and a next development phase planned for 60 acres
- Exit non-core real estate - sale of the entire 26% stake held by the Company in Portus Ventures Private Limited to Adani Airport City Limited, concluded on June 10, 2026, aligning with the GMR Group's strategic intent to focus on real estate opportunities already identified as part of its existing businesses
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: GPUIL is progressing with plans to add a 350 MW Unit 4 at its Kamalanga plant in Odisha, a brownfield addition that benefits from infrastructure already developed during earlier phases including foundations for major equipment and common facilities; long-term PPAs have already been secured for 185.5 MW of that capacity while efforts continue to tie up the balance and advance the project towards implementation. Alongside this, the Company has initiated the development of a renewable energy portfolio spanning solar, Commercial & Industrial (C&I), hybrid and Firm & Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) solutions, incorporating new entities during the year to pursue renewable opportunities across multiple states; the approximately 5 MW solar project at Bhogapuram Airport was successfully commissioned in May 2026, and GMR Andhra Pradesh Renewable Energy - I Limited (GAREL), a wholly owned subsidiary of GEL, has been incorporated as an SPV for a 300 MW renewable energy project in Andhra Pradesh, has applied for ISTS connectivity and is evaluating suitable locations, land availability, evacuation infrastructure and commercial opportunities. In the hydro portfolio, the 900 MW Upper Karnali Hydroelectric Project in Nepal remains an important opportunity with discussions advancing with strategic partners and requisite approvals being pursued; GMR (Badrinath) Hydro Power Generation Private Limited's 300 MW run-of-the-river Alaknanda project in Chamoli district, Uttarakhand has achieved UNFCCC registration as a CDM project, completed possession of required land and obtained key statutory permits, but implementation and financial closure remain stalled by a Supreme Court stay order on 24 hydroelectric projects in Uttarakhand, with the matter listed for final hearing in September 2026; GMR Londa Hydropower Private Limited's 225 MW Talong Londa HEP in East Kameng district, Arunachal Pradesh has received Techno-Economic concurrence from CEA, Defence clearance and in-principle Environmental clearance, with the forest land diversion proposal under process at MoEF & CC and an MoU recently executed with the Government of Assam for formation of a JV including a power off-take arrangement for State captive power. In Smart Energy and Digital Utilities, the Uttar Pradesh smart metering projects executed through GMR Smart Electricity Distribution Private Limited (GSEDPL) had more than 39 lakh smart meters installed as of April 2026 against a contracted scope of 75.69 lakh meters, approximately 3.9 million smart meters installed and integrated by April 2026, an additional variation order for 1.02 Million meters received from the State, and discussions under way for further expansion of the project scope. In urban infrastructure, development activities continued at GMR Krishnagiri Special Investment Region (GKSIR), including infrastructure creation across approximately 61 acres to support future industrial leasing and land monetisation, with 27 acres under discussion for sale to an agency of the Tamil Nadu Government and a third party and the next phase of development being planned for 60 acres. In roads, the DFCC project is completed and the track handed over to DFCCIL for operations, though certain ancillary works remain pending completion.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Rising electricity demand driven by industrialisation, urbanisation, digital infrastructure, electric mobility and growing consumer aspirations, alongside India's clean energy transition through investments in renewable energy, storage solutions, transmission networks and distribution modernisation
- Conventional generation continues to remain critical in ensuring grid stability and meeting baseload requirements even as renewable energy plays an increasingly important role in the future energy mix
- Government policy support - power sector reforms, the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) strengthening distribution through digitalisation and smart metering, measures to accelerate electric mobility, the SHAKTI Bill and a roadmap to develop 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047
- Smart metering is emerging as a critical enabler of distribution reform by improving energy accounting, reducing losses and enhancing overall efficiency of distribution networks, so management believes the digital utility infrastructure opportunity remains substantial
- Sustained public capital expenditure and an enabling policy framework in transportation, urban infrastructure and energy systems are creating significant opportunities for private-sector participation
- Non-fossil sources accounted for over half of the country's installed generation capacity, reflecting the continuing shift towards cleaner sources of energy
- Higher contribution from the coal trading business, driven by increased market demand and higher trading volumes, lifted power segment revenue
- Attractive opportunities are seen in Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE), energy storage, digital utilities and other technology-led solutions supporting a more reliable, flexible and sustainable energy ecosystem
- Strong domestic consumption, sustained public investment, a vibrant services sector and a gradual revival in private capital expenditure provided a solid foundation for India's growth
- Long-term PPAs already secured for 185.5 MW of the planned 350 MW Kamalanga Unit 4 capacity, while efforts continue to tie up the balance capacity
- Uttar Pradesh smart metering contracted scope of 75.69 lakh meters, against which more than 39 lakh smart meters were installed as of April 2026; an additional variation order for 1.02 Million meters has been received from the State and discussions are under way for expansion of the project scope
- GWEL power sales under tied-up PPAs achieved 93.9% of plan, with generation supplied to MSEDCL, TNEB and HPPC in line with scheduling and contractual commitments; balance power was sold to other customers on a merchant basis
- GKEL power sales under tied-up PPAs achieved 93.4% of plan, with generation supplied to Haryana Discoms through PTC, GRIDCO, Bihar and TANGEDCO; balance power was sold to other customers on a merchant basis
- GWEL has long-term fuel supply arrangements with South Eastern Coalfields Limited (SECL) and Western Coalfields Limited (WCL) for entire PPA capacity
- GKEL has long-term fuel supply arrangements with Mahanadi Coalfields Limited (MCL) under Firm Linkage, SHAKTI-II and SHAKTI B-III for entire PPA capacity
- The transportation business continues to operate three highway assets spanning approximately 888 lane kilometres
- GKEL has secured a senior loan facility of Rs 2,700 crore under the refinancing arrangement, enabling the repayment of all existing lenders

litigation.note: The Board's Report describes several material disputes. GKEL had a long-running arbitration with SEPCO over delays in construction and technical issues at the coal-fired thermal power plant, in which the Supreme Court pronounced judgement in GKEL's favour on September 26, 2025; GKEL reversed the liability payable to SEPCO and presented it as an exceptional item. GMR Pochanpalli Expressways Limited (GPEL), a step-down subsidiary, had invoked arbitration against NHAI over the applicability of periodic maintenance (overlay work) under the Concession Agreement, with NHAI having levied penalty and withheld portions of annuity amounts; both parties settled through a Conciliation Committee of Independent Experts (CCIE-2), entering a Settlement Agreement dated February 19, 2026 under section 73 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, following which all pending litigation proceedings were withdrawn. Favourable Supreme Court judgments also enabled recovery of substantial outstanding dues from Haryana DISCOM together with interest and eliminated a significant contingent liability arising from a legacy arbitration dispute. The Alaknanda hydro project of GBHPL remains stalled by a Supreme Court stay order on 24 hydroelectric projects in Uttarakhand, with the matter listed for final hearing in September 2026 and the Company seeking reimbursement of project-related costs from Central and State authorities. Read in the Board's Report / Directors' Report narrative.

risks.risk: Dependence on conventional coal-fired thermal generation for the bulk of earnings
risks.note: The stable earnings base rests on two coal-fired plants (GMR Warora and GMR Kamalanga); the Chairman's message notes India's energy mix is shifting towards renewables, storage and dispatchable solutions even while conventional generation remains critical for grid stability and baseload.

risks.risk: Offtaker / customer curtailment and DISCOM counterparty exposure
risks.note: Reported plant load factors at both thermal plants are stated as 'after customer curtailment', and recovery of long-outstanding dues from Haryana DISCOM required favourable Supreme Court judgments — showing that realisation depends on state distribution utilities.

risks.risk: Legacy litigation, arbitration and contingent liabilities
risks.note: The Board's Report describes multiple long-running disputes — GKEL vs SEPCO arbitration, GPEL vs NHAI periodic-maintenance arbitration settled through a Conciliation Committee of Independent Experts, and a legacy arbitration contingent liability eliminated only by a Supreme Court judgment — indicating recurring exposure to protracted litigation.

Management frames the year around strengthening the balance sheet, resolving legacy obligations through a One-Time Settlement at GREL and refinancing GKEL's senior debt; a further reduction in GKEL's cost of borrowing is stated to be subject to a credit rating upgrade, so financing costs remain rating-dependent.

risks.risk: Regulatory and judicial stoppage of hydro projects
risks.note: GMR (Badrinath) Hydro Power's 300 MW Alaknanda project was construction-ready but implementation and financial closure remain stalled by a Supreme Court stay order on 24 hydroelectric projects in Uttarakhand, causing an 11-year delay described as beyond GMR's control.

risks.risk: Fuel availability and coal price exposure
risks.note: Both thermal plants depend on long-term fuel supply arrangements (SECL/WCL for GWEL; MCL under Firm Linkage, SHAKTI-II and SHAKTI B-III for GKEL); the Board's Report attributes movement in fuel consumption cost to coal prices during the year.

risks.risk: Execution and scope risk in the smart metering build-out
risks.note: The Uttar Pradesh smart metering programme is a large multi-year installation contract with a stated contracted scope against which delivery is still in progress, plus a variation order and further scope-expansion discussions — making revenue recognition contingent on meeting performance obligations.

risks.risk: Early-stage renewable portfolio with unsecured capacity and offtake
risks.note: The renewable, hybrid and FDRE initiatives are described by the Chairman as at an early stage; at the planned 350 MW Kamalanga Unit 4 long-term PPAs are secured for only part of the capacity, with efforts continuing to tie up the balance.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: GMR Power and Urban Infra Limited (GPUIL) is a diversified infrastructure company with interests across Energy, Roads, Smart Meter Infrastructure and Urban Infrastructure businesses, with an operating coal-based generation capacity of 1,650 MW as at March 31, 2026.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: GPUIL generates and sells electricity from coal-fired thermal power plants at Warora (Maharashtra) and Kamalanga (Odisha), supplying state distribution utilities under long-term power purchase agreements and selling balance power to other customers on a merchant basis, alongside a coal trading business and a solar plant at Charanka, Gujarat. The Company is building a Smart Energy and Digital Utilities business, installing and maintaining smart electricity meters for the State of Uttar Pradesh under the Government's distribution reform programme, and is developing a renewable energy portfolio spanning solar, Commercial & Industrial, hybrid and Firm & Dispatchable Renewable Energy solutions plus hydropower projects in India and Nepal. It also operates three highway assets spanning approximately 888 lane kilometres, undertakes EPC work, and develops urban infrastructure at the GMR Krishnagiri Special Investment Region.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Rising electricity demand driven by industrialisation, urbanisation, digital infrastructure, electric mobility and growing consumer aspirations, alongside India's clean energy transition through investments in renewable energy, storage solutions, transmission networks and distribution modernisation
- Conventional generation continues to remain critical in ensuring grid stability and meeting baseload requirements even as renewable energy plays an increasingly important role in the future energy mix
- Government policy support - power sector reforms, the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) strengthening distribution through digitalisation and smart metering, measures to accelerate electric mobility, the SHAKTI Bill and a roadmap to develop 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047
- Smart metering is emerging as a critical enabler of distribution reform by improving energy accounting, reducing losses and enhancing overall efficiency of distribution networks, so management believes the digital utility infrastructure opportunity remains substantial
- Sustained public capital expenditure and an enabling policy framework in transportation, urban infrastructure and energy systems are creating significant opportunities for private-sector participation
- Non-fossil sources accounted for over half of the country's installed generation capacity, reflecting the continuing shift towards cleaner sources of energy
- Higher contribution from the coal trading business, driven by increased market demand and higher trading volumes, lifted power segment revenue
- Attractive opportunities are seen in Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE), energy storage, digital utilities and other technology-led solutions supporting a more reliable, flexible and sustainable energy ecosystem
- Strong domestic consumption, sustained public investment, a vibrant services sector and a gradual revival in private capital expenditure provided a solid foundation for India's growth
- Long-term PPAs already secured for 185.5 MW of the planned 350 MW Kamalanga Unit 4 capacity, while efforts continue to tie up the balance capacity
- Uttar Pradesh smart metering contracted scope of 75.69 lakh meters, against which more than 39 lakh smart meters were installed as of April 2026; an additional variation order for 1.02 Million meters has been received from the State and discussions are under way for expansion of the project scope
- GWEL power sales under tied-up PPAs achieved 93.9% of plan, with generation supplied to MSEDCL, TNEB and HPPC in line with scheduling and contractual commitments; balance power was sold to other customers on a merchant basis
- GKEL power sales under tied-up PPAs achieved 93.4% of plan, with generation supplied to Haryana Discoms through PTC, GRIDCO, Bihar and TANGEDCO; balance power was sold to other customers on a merchant basis
- GWEL has long-term fuel supply arrangements with South Eastern Coalfields Limited (SECL) and Western Coalfields Limited (WCL) for entire PPA capacity
- GKEL has long-term fuel supply arrangements with Mahanadi Coalfields Limited (MCL) under Firm Linkage, SHAKTI-II and SHAKTI B-III for entire PPA capacity
- The transportation business continues to operate three highway assets spanning approximately 888 lane kilometres
- GKEL has secured a senior loan facility of Rs 2,700 crore under the refinancing arrangement, enabling the repayment of all existing lenders

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Portfolio optimisation through monetisation of select non-core energy assets - advancing the stake sale in the Bajoli Holi Hydro Electricity Plant and the Vemagiri & Rajahmundry gas assets under a framework agreement with Synergy Investments Holding Limited, and using proceeds to address legacy obligations and reduce consolidated debt
- Strengthen the balance sheet and financial flexibility - a preferential issuance of equity shares and warrants aggregating to Rs 1,200 crore, refinancing of GKEL's senior debt at improved terms, and resolution of GREL's debt through a One-Time Settlement
- Simplify the group structure - GMR Energy Limited acquired the residual stake in GKEL, making it a wholly owned subsidiary
- Build a renewable energy portfolio spanning solar, Commercial & Industrial (C&I), hybrid and Firm & Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) solutions, with new entities incorporated to pursue opportunities across multiple states
- Scale the Smart Energy and Digital Utilities business on the back of the Uttar Pradesh smart metering programme, positioned as a foundation for long-term, technology-led and recurring revenue streams
- Grow thermal capacity at an existing brownfield site by adding a 350 MW Unit 4 at the Kamalanga plant, leveraging foundations for major equipment and common facilities already developed in earlier phases
- Pursue the hydro portfolio in a calibrated manner with emphasis on project viability, risk management, capital discipline and long-term value creation - advancing the 900 MW Upper Karnali project in Nepal with strategic partners and requisite approvals
- Monetise urban infrastructure land at GMR Krishnagiri Special Investment Region through land sales and industrial leasing, with 27 acres under discussion for sale and a next development phase planned for 60 acres
- Exit non-core real estate - sale of the entire 26% stake held by the Company in Portus Ventures Private Limited to Adani Airport City Limited, concluded on June 10, 2026, aligning with the GMR Group's strategic intent to focus on real estate opportunities already identified as part of its existing businesses
